In the theory of [[permutation pattern]]s, a '''skew-merged permutation''' is a [[permutation]] that can be partitioned into an increasing sequence and a decreasing sequence. They were first studied by {{harvtxt|Stankova|1994}} and given their name by {{harvtxt|Atkinson|1998}}.<ref>{{harvtxt|Stankova|1994}};{{harvtxt|Atkinson|1998}}.</ref>

==Characterization==
The two smallest permutations that cannot be partitioned into an increasing and a decreasing sequence are 3412 and 2143. {{harvtxt|Stankova|1994}} was the first to establish that a skew-merged permutation can also be equivalently defined as a permutation that avoids the two patterns 3412 and 2143.{{sfnp|Stankova|1994}}

A permutation is skew-merged if and only if its associated [[permutation graph]] is a [[split graph]], a graph that can be partitioned into a [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] (corresponding to the descending subsequence) and an [[independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] (corresponding to the ascending subsequence). The two forbidden patterns for skew-merged permutations, 3412 and 2143, correspond to two of the three forbidden [[induced subgraph]]s for split graphs, a four-vertex cycle and a graph with two disjoint edges, respectively. The third forbidden induced subgraph, a five-vertex cycle, cannot exist in a permutation graph.{{sfnp|Kézdy|Snevily|Wang|1996}}

==Enumeration==
For <math>n=1,2,3,\dots</math> the number of skew-merged permutations of length <math>n</math> is
:1, 2, 6, 22, 86, 340, 1340, 5254, 20518, 79932, 311028, 1209916, 4707964, 18330728, ... {{OEIS|A029759}}.

{{harvtxt|Atkinson|1998}} was the first to show that the [[generating function]] of these numbers is
:<math>\frac{1-3x}{(1-2x)\sqrt{1-4x}},</math>
from which it follows that the number of skew-merged permutations of length <math>n</math> is given by the formula
:<math>\binom{2n}{n}-\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}2^{n-m-1}\binom{2m}{m}</math>
and that these numbers obey the [[recurrence relation]]
:<math>P_n=\frac{(9n-8)P_{n-1} - (26n-46)P_{n-2} + (24n-60)P_{n-3}}{n}.</math>
Another derivation of the generating function for skew-merged permutations was given by {{harvtxt|Albert|Vatter|2013}}.{{sfnp|Albert|Vatter|2013}}

==Computational complexity==
Testing whether one permutation is a pattern in another can be solved efficiently when the larger of the two permutations is skew-merged, as shown by {{harvtxt|Albert|Lackner|Lackner|Vatter|2016}}.{{sfnp|Albert|Lackner|Lackner|Vatter|2016}}
